## ASYMPTOMATIC BACTERIURIA
Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in women and elderly people, especially in
those with chronic medical problems (e.g., diabetes, spinal cord injury,
institutionalized patients, catheterized patients). Most patients have no
adverse outcomes and receive no benefit from treatment of asymptomatic
bacteriuria.
Patients who have no symptoms of cystitis (i.e., no dysuria, pain, urgency)
should not be treated. The presence of pyuria (>7 wbc/hpf) or positive leukocyte
esterase, urine nitrate, or urine bacteria is not a sufficient indication for
antibiotic treatment. Screening and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria is
indicated for pregnant women and patients who will have urological procedures
and may be indicated in patients < 1-month post-renal transplant. If an
indwelling catheter is in place and can be removed safely, it should be done as
the bacteriuria may clear.
Bacteriuria in pregnant women is associated with pyelonephritis, premature
delivery, and lower birth weight. Screening for bacteriuria is recommended at
least once early in pregnancy. If bacteriuria is not found upon initial testing,
further screening cultures are not needed. If bacteriuria (>10,000 CFU/mL) is
present, the patient should be treated. Testing should be repeated throughout
the pregnancy to detect recurrences.

## Pregnant women, empirical treatment
## Inpatient Preferred:
[Nitrofurantoin SA 100 mg PO q12h ($) [R,O], CrCl >30 mL/min, for 5 days](psjzid-nitrofurantoin-sa-100-mg-po-bid)
*Avoid nitrofurantoin in the third trimester
Alternatives:
[Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO q12h ($) [R] for 5 days](psjzid-amox-clav-875-125mg-po-q12h)
< OR >
[Cefadroxil 1000 mg q12h ($) [R] for 5 days](psjzid-cefadroxil-1000mg-po-q12h)

## Renal transplant recipients < 1 month after transplant
Screening and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria may be indicated. Consult
nephrology for recommendations.
